submission.natural_language_explanation: Fires on single tokens whose meaning is a concrete physical place or a region of one - terrain (valley, basin, canyon, gorge, cavern) and parts of the built environment (plaza, corridor, street, neighborhood, apartment, balcony, doorway, basement, courtyard, tunnel, depot, villa, elevator) - with Chinese place words (山谷, 城市, 街道, 村庄, 街区) firing as strongly, and graded within that class (measured in a fixed frame: valley 1.13 > plaza 1.01 > corridor 0.84 > canyon 0.66 > street 0.36 > village 0.29 on the scan max of 1.23). It is not a concrete-noun or written-register detector - institution/building words (school, hospital, church, market, bridge, station), ordinary objects and artistic roles (kitchen, table, chair, author, poet, painter) and abstract spatial nouns (place, area, site, zone) all sit at ~0 - so activity is predicted from place-of-space meaning in any language and any context, with three acknowledged offshoot clusters that also fire at 0.3-0.8: extent/position adjectives (spacious, cramped, ample, massive, interior, adjacent, opposite, coastal, urban, suburban), news/publishing role-and-outlet nouns (editor, reporter, columnist, newspaper, bureau, column) and quality adjectives used in property/procedure description (rundown, simple, straightforward).

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Subject: digitisation project, week nine status

Over the past two months the team has scanned, cropped, straightened and indexed roughly forty thousand pages from the collection's back catalogue. The vendor delivered the first batch on schedule, but the optical character recognition was uneven: bold titles came through cleanly, while the dense legal notices and the narrow classified listings produced garbled output that required manual correction. We triaged the failures by page type, rewrote the cleanup rules, and cut the error rate by about half.

Storage planning took longer than expected. The initial estimate assumed compressed images at a fixed bit depth, but the vendor's colour profiles differed from ours, so every batch had to be re-encoded. Because the originals are being kept, the total storage is closer to four terabytes than the one and a half we budgeted. Finance approved the extra capacity last Thursday, conditional on a quarterly review of usage.

Metadata continues to be the slowest part of the work. Each page needs a date, a section label, a page number and a confidence score, and the volunteers have been entering these by hand wherever the automated pass fails. We are testing a review queue that flags low-confidence records for a second pair of eyes; early results suggest it catches most of the bad dates without overwhelming the queue. Two volunteers have asked for clearer guidance on ambiguous headers, and we will circulate a short style note this week.

On staffing, we lost one part-time indexer in July and have not replaced her. The remaining team has absorbed the load by shifting the schedule, but the backlog of unindexed pages has grown by about a thousand. If we want to finish by March, we will need either another indexer or a reduction in scope; both options are in the note attached for the steering group.

The scanning hardware has held up reasonably well. One feeder jammed repeatedly and was repaired under warranty, and the lamp on the second unit was replaced after colour drift became noticeable in the daily calibration targets. We now run a calibration strip at the start of every session and log the readings, which has made batch comparisons much more reliable.

Downstream, the search prototype is working on a subset of twenty thousand pages. Queries for names and dates return sensible results, but phrase search still misses hyphenated compounds, and the relevance ranking favours short pages. Engineering has a fix for the tokenizer scheduled for next sprint; after that we can rerun the evaluation set and compare precision against the vendor's baseline.

Training for the new volunteers begins in two weeks. The session will cover handling, copyright questions and the review queue, and we will record it so that remote contributors can watch later. Please send any corrections to the outline before Friday.

By evening the last crate of bound volumes had been carried down to the cellar, and the crew signed off on the job. The project remains broadly on schedule, though the metadata backlog is the main risk to the March deadline.
